What is AI order entry?
AI order entry reads purchase orders that arrive by email, PDF, spreadsheet or WhatsApp, pulls out the customer, items, quantities and dates, matches them to your item numbers and creates the sales order in your ERP. Orders it is unsure about go to a person to confirm.

How much does it cost?
A fixed fee for a two-week audit, a fixed price for the build quoted in the audit’s spec before you commit, then a flat monthly fee to run it. Never per seat. The price depends mostly on how many order formats and systems are involved.

Which ERPs do you work with?
We build around the ERP you already run, such as Epicor Prophet 21 or Eclipse, Infor, NetSuite, Acumatica, SAP Business One, Microsoft Dynamics or Tally. If it accepts orders through an API, an import file or its database, we can connect to it.

Do we have to change our ERP or how customers order?
No. Customers keep sending orders the way they do today, and orders land in the ERP you already use. Nothing is migrated.

What happens when an order is unclear?
It is not guessed. The line is flagged for a person with the exact question to resolve, such as a unit of measure or an unknown part number, and the answer teaches the system for next time.

How long until it is running?
Two weeks for the audit and three to six weeks to build the first workflow, which runs side by side with your team on real orders before it goes live.

Who owns the software and the data?
You do. The code lives in your repository and your data stays yours. If you stop the monthly service, the system keeps running.

Is it only for distributors?
Distributors are our focus. The same approach works for manufacturers, contractors, logistics and service firms whose work arrives as email and ends as data entry.

# Email order processing: why distributors still retype POs, and how to stop

URL: https://www.boredmutant.com/blog/email-order-processing-for-distributors
Updated: 2026-11-11

Distributors still retype emailed POs because most customers order by email and each one sends a different format, which EDI, web stores and template tools cannot absorb. To stop, put every order into one inbox, have software read each email and attachment, match the customer and items to your ERP records, and create the sales order for a person to approve, with unclear lines flagged as questions instead of guesses.

Ask a customer service lead at a mid-size distributor what their team does all morning and the answer is usually some version of "the inbox." Orders arrive as PDFs, spreadsheets, phone photos and three-line emails, and someone types each one into the ERP. This guide explains why that work has survived every wave of technology, the realistic ways to automate it, and how to work out whether it is worth doing for your business.

If you want the broader picture of AI order entry first, start with our guide to [AI order entry for distributors](/blog/ai-order-entry-for-distributors).

## Why do distributors still retype emailed POs?

Because email is how trade customers like to order, and it has not gone away.

In research with more than 3,500 customers of distributors, Distribution Strategy Group found that about 74% of end users order by email very frequently or frequently. Younger buyers leaned on it most: about 71% of buyers under 25 sent orders by email very frequently, against 37% of those over 55. That study is from 2016, but the direction since has been more channels, not fewer. A 2025 survey of 345 industrial buyers and contractors by Channel Marketing Group and BigCommerce found that 65% had made at least one online purchase that year, up from 45% in 2018. Customers are adding web ordering on top of email, not trading one for the other.

Three things keep the emailed PO alive:

- **The customer's own system produces it.** Many contractors and plants raise POs in their purchasing or ERP software, which prints a PDF and emails it. They are not going to log into your portal to retype what their system already produced.
- **EDI does not reach the long tail.** EDI works well for large trading partners who already run it. Most small and mid-size accounts never will.
- **Email is flexible.** A buyer can add "ship the elbows first" or "same as last Tuesday" in a sentence. No form captures that.

So the problem is not that customers send email. It is that every email has to be read, interpreted and keyed by a person.

## What makes an emailed PO hard to enter?

Reading the document is only part of the job. The slow part is turning the customer's words into your records.

| What arrives | Why it takes time |
|---|---|
| PDF from the customer's purchasing system | Layout differs by customer and changes when they upgrade their software |
| Spreadsheet | Columns are named and ordered differently by every customer |
| Free text in the email body | No structure at all; quantities and items are mixed with notes |
| Scan or phone photo | Has to be read as an image, often skewed or handwritten |
| Customer part numbers | Have to be translated to your item numbers |
| Units like "box", "case", "bundle" | Mean different quantities for different customers and items |
| Changes and follow-ups | "Please add 2 more to PO 4471" has to find and change an existing order |

Every row on that table is a judgment call a good rep makes many times a day. An email order processing system is only useful if it makes the same calls, or asks when it can't.

## What are your options for email order processing?

There are four broad approaches. They are not mutually exclusive; many distributors combine them.

| Approach | How it works | Good fit | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Email parsers and workflow tools | Rules extract fields from emails and send them on to other apps (Mailparser, for example, builds parsing rules with a setup wizard and passes data on through Zapier or webhooks) | A few customers with consistent emails | Rules need upkeep as formats change; matching to your items is up to you |
| Agents built into the ERP | The ERP vendor's own assistant watches a mailbox and drafts quotes or orders | You run that ERP and your orders are fairly simple | Check what it reads, what it can create, and its known limits |
| Order automation platforms | A subscription service that reads orders, matches them and posts them to your ERP | High volume and a mainstream ERP with a ready connector | Pricing usually grows with volume; you rent it |
| Built and owned | A pipeline built around your inbox, your customers and your ERP | Unusual formats, units or a customized ERP, or you want to own it | Needs a build period and a parallel run |

A few specifics, so you can compare like with like:

- **Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central** has a Sales Order Agent that monitors a mailbox, verifies the customer, checks item availability, creates a sales quote and drafts a reply with the quote attached as a PDF. Microsoft's documentation lists the points where a person reviews the work, and is open about limits: for example, items with non-base units of measure can come out with the wrong quantity.
- **Dynamics 365 Finance & Supply Chain Management** has a sales order agent that, according to Microsoft partner Sikich, monitors a mailbox for PDF and image attachments, extracts the purchase order details and creates the sales order.
- **Conexiom** is one of the longer-standing platforms. It reports that its customers process more than 80% of transactions without manual touches; treat that as a vendor figure and test it on your own orders.

None of these is wrong. The question is which one copes with your customers' actual emails, which is why the test at the end of this guide matters more than any feature list.

## How does an email become a sales order?

Whatever you buy or build, the work breaks into the same steps. Use this as a checklist when you talk to vendors.

1. **Capture.** Every order goes to one monitored inbox (orders@ or similar), with reps forwarding anything that lands in a personal inbox. Modern systems get new mail through push notifications: Microsoft Graph sends change notifications for messages in a mailbox, and the Gmail API's watch method publishes mailbox changes to Google Cloud Pub/Sub.
2. **Sort.** Not every email is an order. The system separates new orders from changes, cancellations, quote requests and "where is my order" questions, and routes each one.
3. **Read.** It pulls the header (customer, PO number, ship-to, dates, notes) and every line (item, quantity, unit, price) from the body and every attachment.
4. **Match.** It finds the customer and ship-to account, then translates each line to your item number using cross-references, order history and descriptions. Your ERP's own tools matter here. NetSuite, for example, has a Customer Part Numbers feature for importing sales orders by the customer's part numbers, and its documentation notes that an invalid or unknown part number makes the import for that transaction fail. Catching those before they reach the ERP is part of the job.
5. **Check.** It compares prices, units, minimums and availability against what your team checks today, and flags differences rather than quietly changing them.
6. **Review.** A person approves the order, or answers the specific question the system raised ("Line 3: customer part 4471-B matches two items"). Early on, every order is reviewed. Later, clean orders from trusted customers can go straight in.
7. **Write to the ERP.** The order goes in through whatever route the ERP supports. For Epicor Prophet 21, integration firm Airdev describes three native routes: scheduled flat-file import, EDI 850s and the separately licensed Transaction API. Airdev also notes that P21 has no native path for customer PDFs or emailed orders, which is exactly the gap this step fills.
8. **Confirm.** The customer gets an acknowledgment, and the email thread is linked to the order so anyone can see what was asked for.

## Running an old inbox script? Check it now

Some distributors already have a homegrown script or an older tool that reads the orders mailbox through Exchange Web Services (EWS). If your mail is in Microsoft 365, that script is on a deadline. Microsoft began disabling EWS in Exchange Online by default on October 1, 2026, and says that after April 1, 2027, EWS access will be permanently removed with no way to turn it back on. Until then, tenants can keep EWS running only for an approved list of apps.

The replacement is Microsoft Graph, and Microsoft's own migration guidance notes that it works differently: notifications arrive by webhook, and some EWS features have no direct equivalent, so tools may need redesigning rather than a quick patch. Ask whoever maintains your order inbox tooling which API it uses.

## What does it cost to keep retyping?

Two numbers matter: time and errors.

**Time.** Use this formula with your own figures:

**Yearly hours = orders per day × minutes per order × working days ÷ 60**

Say your team enters 80 emailed orders a day at 8 minutes each, 250 working days a year. That is 2,667 hours a year, more than one full-time person spent only on typing. At $32 an hour fully loaded, it is about $85,000 a year. The calculator on our [home page](/#cost) runs this with your numbers.

**Errors.** Manual keying is accurate most of the time, but not all of the time. Conexiom's review of the research describes about 1% as the figure most often cited as the ceiling for acceptable manual data entry. Measured rates can be higher: a 2019 study in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association found a 3.7% error rate when clinic staff typed test results into records by hand.

Here is what 1% looks like for the same distributor, as an illustration. If the average order has 6 lines, 80 orders a day is 480 keyed lines. At 1%, that is about 5 wrong lines a day, or about 1,200 a year. Some are caught before shipping. The rest become wrong deliveries, credit memos, return freight and an awkward call with a customer.

To get your real numbers, time ten ordinary orders from opening the email to saving the order, and count last quarter's credit memos caused by entry mistakes.

## How to get started this month

You can do the groundwork before choosing any tool:

1. **Consolidate.** Route all orders to one shared inbox and ask reps to forward stragglers.
2. **Sample.** Save one week of orders and tag each one: clean PDF, spreadsheet, free text, scan, customer part numbers, odd units.
3. **Measure.** Time ten orders and note the slowest steps. It is usually matching items, not typing.
4. **Clean the cross-references.** List your top 20 customers' part numbers and units against your items. Every approach above relies on this data.
5. **Test before you sign.** Give any vendor, including us, ten real orders including your worst one, and count three things: orders that would have gone in untouched, orders flagged with the right question, and orders that went in wrong without a flag. The last number is the one that matters.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is email order processing?

Email order processing is the work of turning purchase orders that customers email (in the message body or as PDF, spreadsheet or image attachments) into sales orders in your ERP. Automated email order processing uses software to read each email, match the customer and items to your records and create the order for a person to approve.

### Can email orders be entered into the ERP automatically?

Yes. Software can read emailed POs, match them to your customers and items and create the sales order through the ERP's API, import files or another supported route. Most teams start with a person approving every order, then let clean orders from trusted customers go straight in once accuracy is proven on their own orders.

### Is an email parser enough?

An email parser works when a few customers send consistent emails. It extracts fields but usually does not match customer part numbers or units to your items, and its rules need updating when a customer changes format. For many customers and formats you need matching and exception handling, not just extraction.

### Do customers have to change how they send orders?

No. The point of automating email orders is that customers keep ordering the way they do today. The only change most distributors make is asking customers to send orders to one shared address.

### What happens when the software is not sure about a line?

A good system does not guess. It holds the order and asks a person a specific question, such as which of two items a customer part number means, and remembers the answer so the same question does not come up again.

### Our order inbox script uses EWS. Do we need to act?

If your mailbox is in Microsoft 365, yes. Microsoft started disabling EWS in Exchange Online by default on October 1, 2026, and plans to remove it permanently after April 1, 2027. Tools that read the inbox through EWS need to move to Microsoft Graph.

# AI order entry for distributors: how it works, what it costs, and how to judge it

URL: https://www.boredmutant.com/blog/ai-order-entry-for-distributors
Updated: 2026-11-10

AI order entry is software that reads the purchase orders customers email to a distributor (in the email body, PDFs, spreadsheets or scans), pulls out the customer, items, quantities, prices and dates, matches them to the distributor's own customer and item records, and creates the sales order in the ERP. Lines it is unsure about go to a person with the exact question to resolve, so nothing is guessed.

Most distributors have an online store, an EDI connection for their biggest accounts, and a customer service team that still spends its day reading PDFs and typing them into the ERP. This guide explains what AI order entry does about that, what it costs to leave things as they are, and how to tell a real system from a demo.

## Why order entry is still manual

Customers order the way that suits them, and for trade buyers that is usually email. In customer research from Distribution Strategy Group, about 74% of end users said they order by email very frequently or frequently, either in the body of the email or as a PDF, Word or Excel attachment. Order-automation vendor Conexiom puts the share of B2B orders still emailed to customer service reps at 49%. The exact number varies by sector, but the pattern is the same everywhere: e-commerce and EDI cover some customers, and email covers the rest.

Email orders are hard to automate because no two customers send the same thing. One contractor sends a clean PDF from their purchasing system, another types "same as last week plus 2 cases of the 3/4 elbows" into the body, a third attaches a spreadsheet with their own part numbers. Older tools could not cope with that variety. Template-based OCR breaks when a customer changes their form, and screen-recording bots (RPA) only automate the typing, not the reading.

## How AI order entry works, step by step

A working system does the same job a good customer service rep does, in the same order:

1. **Capture.** It watches the orders inbox (or a shared mailbox, fax-to-email line or portal upload) and picks up every new order, including attachments.
2. **Read.** It reads the document the way a person would: the email body, PDFs, scans, spreadsheets and Word files. It pulls out the header (customer, PO number, ship-to, requested date, notes) and every line (item, quantity, unit of measure, price).
3. **Match the customer.** It finds the account and ship-to in the ERP, using the sender, the PO's bill-to and ship-to addresses and the customer's history.
4. **Match the items.** This is the hard part. Customers use their own part numbers, manufacturer numbers, descriptions or nicknames. The system matches each line to your item number using your cross-reference tables, the customer's order history and the product description, and converts units (a "box" from one customer is 25 each, from another it is 100).
5. **Check.** It compares price, minimum order quantity, availability and anything else your team checks today, and flags differences instead of quietly fixing them.
6. **Score confidence.** Every field gets a confidence level. Orders where everything matches go straight in. Orders with a doubt go to a person, with the doubt spelled out: "Line 3: customer part 4471-B has two possible matches."
7. **Enter.** It creates the sales order in the ERP through whatever the ERP supports: an API, an import file or a staging table.
8. **Learn.** When a person resolves a question, the answer is saved, so the same customer part number never needs a human again.

The result is not "no people". It is people spending their time on the orders that need judgment instead of typing the ones that do not.

## What it is not

| Approach | What it does | Where it breaks |
|---|---|---|
| EDI | Exchanges structured orders with trading partners who support it | Most small and mid-size customers will never set it up |
| E-commerce portal | Lets customers order on your site | Customers who prefer email keep emailing |
| Template OCR | Reads fixed positions on known forms | Breaks when a form changes; cannot read free-text emails |
| RPA bots | Copies data from one screen to another | Still needs clean data; does not read or match anything |
| AI order entry | Reads any format, matches to your records, enters the order, flags doubts | Needs good item and customer data to match against, and a person for real exceptions |

None of these replace each other. AI order entry is for the orders that arrive by email and will keep arriving by email.

## What manual order entry costs you

You can put a number on it with four inputs:

**Yearly hours = orders per day × minutes per order × working days ÷ 60**

Take a distributor entering 80 orders a day at 8 minutes each, 250 days a year. That is 2,667 hours of typing a year, more than one full-time person. At $32 an hour fully loaded, it is about $85,000 a year. The calculator on our [home page](/#cost) runs the same sum with your own numbers.

That figure leaves out the costs that do not show up on the payroll: keying errors that become wrong shipments and credit memos, orders that miss the truck because they sat in the inbox, and reps who cannot quote or call customers because they are typing.

To get your real minutes per order, time it. Pick ten ordinary orders, not the easy ones, and time a rep from opening the email to saving the order. Most teams underestimate this number until they measure it.

## Buy a platform or build your own

There are two broad ways to get AI order entry.

**Buy a platform.** Several companies sell order automation as a subscription. Conexiom, which has been in sales order automation for years, says 16 of North America's 20 largest distributors use it. Canals, which started with AI sales order entry and now covers more distributor workflows, raised a $35 million Series A in May 2026 and says more than 100 distributors use its software. ERP vendors and their partners are also adding order capture features.

**Have it built around your systems.** A smaller firm (like us) builds the same pipeline for your inbox, your customers and your ERP, and you own the code.

| | Platform subscription | Built and owned |
|---|---|---|
| Time to start | Fast if your ERP has a ready connector | A few weeks, including a parallel run |
| Pricing | Usually quote-based, often by volume or tier, ongoing | Fixed build price, then an optional monthly fee to run it |
| Fit to your quirks | Configurable within the product | Built around your rules, units and exceptions |
| Ownership | You rent it | You own the code and the data |
| Best when | High volume, a standard ERP, and you want a vendor to own the roadmap | Unusual formats, an older or customized ERP, or you want the system as an asset |

Neither is right for everyone. If your ERP is mainstream and the platform's connector already exists, a subscription can be the faster path. If your orders, units or ERP are unusual, or you would rather not pay per order forever, building makes sense.

## How the order gets into your ERP

Most distribution ERPs offer at least one of three ways in:

- **An API.** NetSuite (SuiteTalk), SAP Business One (Service Layer), Acumatica (REST API) and Epicor Prophet 21 (through its middleware server) all expose ways for other software to create sales orders.
- **An import file.** Many ERPs accept orders as a CSV or XML file dropped in a folder or loaded on a schedule.
- **A staging table.** On-premise ERPs can often read orders from a database table that the order entry system writes to.

The route matters less than two questions: can the system read your customer, ship-to and item records to match against, and can it write an order the way your team would, with the same defaults, so nobody has to fix it afterwards?

## How to judge any AI order entry system: the 10-PO test

Demos use clean documents. Your inbox does not. Before you sign anything, run this test with any vendor, including us:

1. Pull ten real orders from last week: a clean PDF, a spreadsheet, a free-text email, a scan, one with customer part numbers, one with an odd unit of measure, and your worst one.
2. Ask the vendor to process them and show you the resulting order lines next to your rep's version.
3. Count three numbers: orders that would have gone in with no changes, orders that were flagged with the right question, and orders that went in wrong without a flag.

The third number is the one that matters most. A system that flags a lot is annoying. A system that is confidently wrong ships the wrong goods.

Ask these questions too:

- What happens when it is not sure? (You want a clear question for a person, never a guess.)
- Who sees and approves orders at the start, and how do we move to straight-through processing?
- What does it do with a unit of measure it has not seen?
- Is there a record of what it read, what it changed and who approved it?
- Who owns the data and the configuration if we stop?
- How is it priced, and what happens to the price when our volume doubles?

## A sensible rollout

1. **Audit (about two weeks).** Sit with the people who enter orders, time each step, collect sample orders from your top customers, and agree what "done" looks like.
2. **Build and connect (three to six weeks).** Connect the inbox and the ERP, load cross-references and rules, and process last month's orders as a test.
3. **Run in parallel.** The system prepares every order and your team checks it before it is saved. You see the accuracy on your own orders before anything goes in automatically.
4. **Switch on, customer by customer.** Start with the customers whose orders it handles best. Widen as the numbers hold up.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is AI order entry?

AI order entry is software that reads purchase orders arriving by email, PDF, spreadsheet or scan, pulls out the customer, items, quantities and dates, matches them to the distributor's own records and creates the sales order in the ERP. Orders it is unsure about go to a person with a specific question.

### How accurate is AI order entry?

It depends mostly on how good your item and customer data are and how messy your orders are, which is why you should test it on your own orders. A good system tells you when it is unsure instead of guessing, so the error rate that matters is the share of orders that go in wrong without a flag.

### Do our customers have to change how they order?

No. Customers keep emailing orders in whatever format they use today. The system adapts to them.

### Will it replace our customer service team?

It replaces the typing, not the people. Teams use the time for quotes, follow-ups, problem orders and calls that win business. Exceptions still need someone who knows the customers.

### How much does AI order entry cost?

Platforms are usually priced by quote, often by order volume or tier. A built system is usually a fixed project price plus an optional monthly fee. Compare either against your own cost of manual entry: orders per day, times minutes per order, times working days, times your hourly cost.

### How long does it take to set up?

Plan on a couple of weeks to audit your orders, a few weeks to connect and test, then a period running in parallel with your team before anything goes in on its own.
